explanations.explanation: Four great beasts, friend. The winds churn the sea and up they come, and Daniel says each one is different from the others. I like a surprise, but four of them out of one sea is a lot of surprises. I'd be checking the water before I got anywhere near it.

Those cows belong to another dream. Pharaoh, Egypt's king, dreamed of seven cows coming up from the Nile (Genesis 41:2). Daniel's sea gives up something very different: four great beasts. Same idea of things rising out of water, but different dreamer and different creatures.

A great fish shows up in Jonah's story. Jonah, a prophet, was swallowed by one that the LORD appointed (Jonah 1:17). Daniel's sea sends up four great beasts instead. If a fish had come up, that would have been the easy part of this vision.

Not quite, baker. Daniel says the beasts came up out of the sea, “each one different from the others.” So there's no matching set here. Four beasts, four different looks, and the text lines them up one at a time.

Right, they don't look alike. Daniel says they came up out of the sea, “each one different from the others.” A lion-like one, a bear-like one, a leopard-like one, and a fourth unlike all the rest are coming. Nobody's confusing these four in a lineup.

Torn off is right. Daniel says, “I watched until its wings were torn off.” The beast starts out looking ready to fly and ends up grounded. It's the kind of morning I have when I forget to set the timer.
No fire for these wings. Daniel says, “I watched until its wings were torn off.” Fire does show up later in his vision, but around a throne. Here the wings are simply gone.

The wings don't spread out, friend. Daniel says he watched “until its wings were torn off.” After that the beast is lifted up from the ground. The sea is already busy enough in this vision without extra wings.

Man is right. The beast is made to stand on two feet like a man and given the mind of a man. The wings come off, and the beast goes through a big change. Hang onto that one, because this vision has plenty of changes.

You'd think so, since it's a beast. But the text says it's made to stand on two feet like a man and is given the mind of a man. So the beast gets something new after the wings are gone. It doesn't stay as it was.
There's no child in this verse, friend. The beast is made to stand on two feet like a man and given the mind of a man. The text keeps it grown-up and plain. Daniel just reports what he sees.

explanations.answer: Get up and gorge on flesh
explanations.explanation: That's it. The beast is told, “Get up and gorge yourself on flesh!” Three ribs between its teeth, and it still gets orders for more. The text says it was told, and it doesn't say who by, so I'll leave that open too.
Lying down is the opposite of what happens. The beast is already raised up on one of its sides. Then it's told, “Get up and gorge yourself on flesh!” This one isn't going anywhere to rest.

explanations.answer: Go back down into the sea
explanations.explanation: Nobody sends it back down, baker. The beast has come up out of the sea, and it's told, “Get up and gorge yourself on flesh!” So the command is about getting up and eating. The sea is behind it now.

True. Daniel says of the leopard-like beast, “it was given authority to rule.” It gets four wings and four heads and authority on top of that. The text says it was given authority, and it doesn't say by whom.
It's the other way around, friend. Daniel says of the leopard-like beast, “it was given authority to rule.” Four heads and four wings, and now authority too. This beast is not short on equipment.

Tramples it underfoot, yes. Daniel says the fourth beast “devoured and crushed; then it trampled underfoot whatever was left.” First the teeth, then the feet. I don't think anything gets left over after that.

The sea isn't part of this one. Daniel says the fourth beast “devoured and crushed; then it trampled underfoot whatever was left.” Nothing gets dragged anywhere. It happens right where the beast stands.

explanations.answer: Leaves it for the other beasts
explanations.explanation: No sharing in this verse, baker. Daniel says the fourth beast “devoured and crushed; then it trampled underfoot whatever was left.” The leftovers get trampled. The beast was also different from all the beasts before it, so I wouldn't picture it being generous.
That's right. Three of the first horns “were uprooted before it,” Daniel says. The little horn comes up and three of the ten are gone. For a little one, it makes itself felt in a hurry.
Not here, friend. The text says three of the first horns “were uprooted before it.” They don't grow into anything. They're pulled out when the little horn comes up.
No crowns in this verse. Daniel says three of the first horns “were uprooted before it.” They don't change into anything. They simply come out.
Arrogance is right. The horn has eyes like those of a man and a mouth that spoke words of arrogance. Daniel looks at it closely, and it's talking big. I'd keep an eye on that mouth too.

Comfort would be nice, baker, but that's not what comes out. The horn has a mouth that spoke words of arrogance. Daniel keeps watching because of those words (Daniel 7:11). So this horn is not the soothing type.
Not prayer, friend. The little horn has a mouth that spoke words of arrogance. That's what holds Daniel's attention. So it's loud, and not in a good way.

True. Daniel says, “A river of fire was flowing, coming out from His presence.” The throne is already flaming with fire, with its wheels ablaze. So the whole scene is lit up around the Ancient of Days.

It's true, friend. Daniel says, “A river of fire was flowing, coming out from His presence.” It's part of the scene around the Ancient of Days. His throne is flaming, and the river runs from where He is.

Thousands upon thousands, yes. Daniel says, “Thousands upon thousands attended Him, and myriads upon myriads stood before Him.” That's a crowd far past counting. Imagine me trying to bake for that many.

Twenty-four elders are from a different vision. John, who wrote Revelation, sees twenty-four elders seated around a throne (Revelation 4:4). Daniel's text gives a much bigger crowd: thousands upon thousands attend the Ancient of Days. His line is a different one than John's.

Seventy elders are on Mount Sinai in another story. Moses, Israel's leader, went up with Aaron, Nadab, Abihu and seventy elders of Israel (Exodus 24:9). Daniel's vision has a far bigger crowd. Thousands upon thousands attend the Ancient of Days.

explanations.answer: It's slain and thrown into the fire
explanations.explanation: Yes. Daniel says, “the beast was slain, and its body was destroyed and thrown into the blazing fire.” He kept watching because of the arrogant words, and this is what he saw. The loud horn doesn't get the last word.

explanations.answer: It flees back into the great sea
explanations.explanation: There's no escaping here, baker. Daniel says, “the beast was slain, and its body was destroyed and thrown into the blazing fire.” The beast doesn't get away. The sea is out of the picture by now.

explanations.answer: It bows down before the throne
explanations.explanation: No bowing is mentioned, friend. Daniel says, “the beast was slain, and its body was destroyed and thrown into the blazing fire.” That's the end of that beast. The text doesn't give it a speech or a chance to kneel.

True. Daniel says, “As for the rest of the beasts, their dominion was removed, but they were granted an extension of life for a season and a time.” Their rule is taken away, and their lives go on for a while. The text doesn't say more than that, so neither will I.

This one's true, friend. Daniel says, “As for the rest of the beasts, their dominion was removed, but they were granted an extension of life for a season and a time.” They lose their rule. They still get that extension of life for a while.

Serve is right. He's given dominion, glory and kingship, “that the people of every nation and language should serve Him.” That's every nation and every language. It's about as wide as a cookie box can't be.
No fighting in this verse. The text says that “the people of every nation and language should serve Him.” This One is given dominion, glory and kingship. The word is serve.

Judging is close to the courtroom scene, but this verse says something else. He's given dominion, glory and kingship, “that the people of every nation and language should serve Him.” Every nation and language is in view. So the word is serve.

explanations.answer: One that will never be destroyed
explanations.explanation: That's right. Daniel says, “His kingdom is one that will never be destroyed.” His dominion is everlasting and will not pass away. Compare that with the beasts, who got a season and a time.

explanations.answer: One that lasts for a season
explanations.explanation: A season is what the other beasts got, baker. Daniel says they were granted “an extension of life for a season and a time” (Daniel 7:12). His own kingdom is the opposite: “His kingdom is one that will never be destroyed.” It's an everlasting dominion.

explanations.answer: One that is shared with the beasts
explanations.explanation: The beasts don't share in it, friend. Their dominion was removed (Daniel 7:12). Daniel says of this One, “His kingdom is one that will never be destroyed.” It's His, and it lasts.

explanations.answer: Asks someone standing there what it means
explanations.explanation: That's it. Daniel says, “I approached one of those who were standing there, and I asked him the true meaning of all this.” He doesn't sit with his alarm. He goes and asks someone, and I think that's wise.

explanations.answer: Calls for the wise men of Babylon
explanations.explanation: Calling the wise men is what a king did earlier. Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, summoned them over his dream (Daniel 2:2). Here Daniel goes to one of those standing there. No one gets sent for.

Daniel did pray toward Jerusalem once, with his windows open (Daniel 6:10). That's not what this verse says. Here he approaches one of those standing there and asks the true meaning of all this. The question comes first.

The text says something else. The one explaining says the four great beasts are four kings who will arise from the earth. Then he says, “But the saints of the Most High will receive the kingdom and possess it forever.” The kingdom goes to the saints, not the four kings.

False is right. The explainer says the four beasts are four kings who will arise from the earth. Then he says, “But the saints of the Most High will receive the kingdom and possess it forever.” The saints receive it.

Forever and ever, baker. The explainer says the saints “will receive the kingdom and possess it forever—yes, forever and ever.” He says it twice so you can't miss it. That's the kind of repeating I can get behind.
One generation is far too short. The saints of the Most High “will receive the kingdom and possess it forever—yes, forever and ever.” The text doesn't set a limit. It goes the other direction.
No seven years here, friend. The explainer says the saints “will receive the kingdom and possess it forever—yes, forever and ever.” It's a lot more than seven years. This one doesn't run out.

explanations.answer: The saints of the Most High
explanations.explanation: Yes. Daniel says, “this horn was waging war against the saints and prevailing against them.” This is a heavy part of the vision. The Most High is God, and these are His people.
The other beasts aren't in this fight. Daniel says, “this horn was waging war against the saints and prevailing against them.” It's a heavy moment. The war is aimed at the saints.

explanations.answer: The rest of the ten horns
explanations.explanation: The ten horns aren't the target. Daniel says this horn was “waging war against the saints and prevailing against them.” Three of the first horns were uprooted before it earlier (Daniel 7:8). The war here is against the saints.

True, and I think it's a hard line to read. Daniel says the horn was “waging war against the saints and prevailing against them.” But keep going, because the verse after that has a turn. It's the turn that matters.
It's true, friend, and I think it's a hard one. Daniel says the horn was “waging war against the saints and prevailing against them.” But the next verse tells how it changes. It doesn't stop here.

The Ancient of Days is right. Daniel says He “arrived and pronounced judgment in favor of the saints of the Most High.” Then the time came for them to possess the kingdom. That's the UNTIL, and He's the one in it.

Gabriel does show up in Daniel's book. He's the angel who explains a later vision to Daniel (Daniel 8:16). In this verse, though, it's the Ancient of Days who arrives. He's the one who pronounces judgment in favor of the saints.
Darius the Mede took the kingdom after Belshazzar (Daniel 5:30-31). He isn't in this verse. The one who arrives is the Ancient of Days. He pronounces judgment in favor of the saints of the Most High.

explanations.answer: Ten kings who rise from it
explanations.explanation: Ten kings, yes. The explainer says, “the ten horns are ten kings who will rise from this kingdom.” So the horns on the beast's head stand for kings. They come out of the fourth kingdom.
No cities are named in the explanation. The explainer says, “the ten horns are ten kings who will rise from this kingdom.” So the horns stand for kings. And they rise from the kingdom itself.

Laws do come up later, baker. The king after the ten kings intends to change the appointed times and laws (Daniel 7:25). But the ten horns aren't laws. The explainer says they're ten kings who will rise from this kingdom.
Not quite. The explainer says, “After them another king, different from the earlier ones, will rise and subdue three kings.” So he isn't just like the others. He's different from the earlier ones.
False is right. The explainer says another king will rise after the ten, “different from the earlier ones.” He will also subdue three kings. This one doesn't match the rest.

explanations.answer: A time and times and half a time
explanations.explanation: That's right. The explainer says the saints “will be given into his hand for a time, and times, and half a time.” It's a heavy stretch, and the text gives it in exactly those words. I won't try to turn it into a number, and neither will you.

Forty days and forty nights is how long the rain fell in Noah's flood (Genesis 7:12). That's a different story. Here the explainer says the saints will be given into his hand “for a time, and times, and half a time.” The words are different on purpose.

explanations.answer: Seventy years in a foreign land
explanations.explanation: Seventy years was the length given for Babylon in Jeremiah, a prophet (Jeremiah 29:10). That's not what this verse says. The explainer says the saints “will be given into his hand for a time, and times, and half a time.” That's the phrase to keep.

explanations.answer: It's taken away and destroyed forever
explanations.explanation: Yes. The explainer says, “But the court will convene, and his dominion will be taken away and completely destroyed forever.” The court sits, and the horn's rule is gone. The big talker doesn't come out ahead.

explanations.answer: It's handed over to another king
explanations.explanation: No other king gets it. The explainer says his dominion “will be taken away and completely destroyed forever.” It isn't passed along. The next verse says who does receive the kingdom.

explanations.answer: It's extended for many more years
explanations.explanation: No extension for this one, friend. The explainer says, “But the court will convene, and his dominion will be taken away and completely destroyed forever.” The earlier beasts got an extension of life (Daniel 7:12). This dominion doesn't.
Pale is right. Daniel says, “my thoughts troubled me greatly, and my face turned pale.” That's the face of a man who just saw all that. I'd probably need to sit down too.
Red would be a different kind of reaction. Daniel says, “my thoughts troubled me greatly, and my face turned pale.” The color drains out. It doesn't flush in.
Not radiant, baker. Daniel says, “my thoughts troubled me greatly, and my face turned pale.” His face turns pale after everything he saw and heard. I think he's still taking it in.
He keeps it to himself, friend. Daniel says, “But I kept the matter to myself.” The text doesn't tell us why, so I won't guess. It leaves it at that.
This passage doesn't say Daniel told the king. It opens in Belshazzar's first year (Daniel 7:1). It ends with Daniel saying, “But I kept the matter to myself.” That's the last word we get.
Daniel did tell his friends about a matter once. In Daniel 2:17 he told Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah about the king's dream. Here it's different. He says, “But I kept the matter to myself.”
